Plutocrat

PLOO-tuh-krat · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Plutocrat is a person whose power and influence come from their wealth; a member of a wealthy ruling class.

The documentary argued that a handful of plutocrats now controlled more political influence than most elected officials.

Worked Example

Historians describe the late 1800s in America as an age of plutocrats, when a few oil and railroad tycoons quietly shaped national policy.

A plutocrat's power doesn't come from a title or a vote -- it comes purely from having enormous amounts of money.

How Plutocrat Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

tycoon

tycoon: a wealthy and powerful businessperson

magnate

magnate: a wealthy and influential person, especially in industry

Antonyms

pauper

pauper: a very poor person

peon

peon: a lowly worker with little status or power

How Strong Is It? — wealthy → oligarch → plutocrat

wealthy vs. plutocrat

wealthy vs. plutocrat: Wealthy simply means having a lot of money -- it says nothing about using that money to control politics or society.

oligarch vs. plutocrat

oligarch vs. plutocrat: An oligarch is even more extreme -- one of a very small group that holds nearly total political and economic control over a country.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of plutocrat.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — plout-

root — plout-: wealth (Greek ploutos, 'wealth')

suffix — -crat

suffix — -crat: one who rules or has power (Greek kratos, 'power, rule')

Put it together

Put it together: Plutocrat comes from Greek ploutos ('wealth') + -crat ('ruler') -- literally 'wealth-ruler,' someone who rules or wields power because of their riches.

Use the root in a new word: autocrat

Use the root in a new word: autocrat: Unlike a plutocrat, whose power comes from money, an autocrat rules alone with absolute, unchecked power.

Root Check

Word Choice

Plutocrat is almost always a critical word -- people rarely call themselves plutocrats. It's usually used to accuse someone of using money to buy influence they shouldn't have. (This unit's aristocrat, by contrast, holds power through birth and title, not necessarily wealth.)
